mappings.note: Names metals by an extreme melting point - a physical property of the classification set, with no reactivity or extraction content.

Tests the exception to 'metal + acid gives hydrogen' (nitric acid oxidises instead). The discrimination is between acids, not between metals, so this stays with the LO-1 chemical-property clause rather than the reactivity series.
Malleability superlative - physical-property recall, the ordering principle is not reactivity so LO-2 does not apply.
WEAK FIT. Pure recall of the aqua-regia recipe and ratio. No outcome covers reagent composition; LO-1 taken because the underlying fact is that noble metals resist ordinary acids.
One metal and one non-metal identified by physical state - LO-1 classification in its most direct form.

Requires knowing an ionic bond forms between a metal and a non-metal, so HCl and CCl4 are excluded. Cited at competency level because C 1.1 explicitly covers how compounds are formed from atomic structure and valency, while neither LO-1 nor LO-2 mentions bonding at all - see the reported outcome-layer gap.
Identifies carbon from allotrope properties - hardness and electrical conductivity. Graphite is the standard exception used when classifying by physical properties, which is LO-1's territory.

Properties of ionic compounds (no conduction in the solid state). LO-1 is about classifying elements, not compounds, so the competency is the closest legal code; the outcome layer has no ionic-compound outcome.
The basic nature of metal oxides is the standard chemical test that separates metals from non-metals - LO-1's chemical-property clause.

Occurrence in the native state is the ores half of LO-6, but the discriminator between Cu/Au/Zn/Ag is position at the bottom of the reactivity series, so LO-2 is cited second. LO-6 leads because the item is about how metals are found, not about predicting a reaction.

POOR FIT - likely a misfiled item. Defining alkalis belongs to acids, bases and salts, not to metals and non-metals. LO-1 is the nearest legal code only because metal oxides and hydroxides are the basic species referred to.
Refining is the final stage of extracting a metal from its ore, and LO-6 is the only outcome covering the metallurgical sequence. No corrosion or reactivity-prediction content here.
Amphoteric oxides are the boundary case in the metal/non-metal chemical classification, so they sit under LO-1's chemical-property clause rather than under any extraction or corrosion outcome.
Blackening of silver is tarnishing, and the item asks for the corrosion product. LO-7's 'explains corrosion' half, not its prevention half.
What one named metal does on ignition - a single-substance chemical property. Nothing is ranked, so LO-2 is not engaged.
Galvanisation is named verbatim in LO-7; the item asks which metal is used for the coating, i.e. the prevention method.
Iron's own behaviour on strong heating. Chosen over LO-2 because the stem names only iron and asks what is observed, not how iron ranks against another metal.
Stainless steel is the textbook case of alloying to resist corrosion, so this composition item lands inside LO-7's explicit 'including ... alloying' clause rather than merely near it.
Copper's own reaction with air on heating and the identity of the black coating. Single-substance chemical property; contrast with the copper-in-open-air item, which is corrosion over time.

Green basic copper carbonate on long exposure to moist air is corrosion, and the item asks for the corrosion product - LO-7 rather than the LO-1 reading of 'copper reacts with air' used for the heated-copper item.
Selecting the metals that resist air even when hot means picking from the bottom of the reactivity series; the item is answered by ranking, not by describing one metal's reaction, so LO-2 over LO-1.
Physical state as the exception among metals - LO-1 classification by physical property.
States the general metal + water reaction as a class property. No particular metals are compared, so this is LO-1's chemical-property clause rather than the series.

Asks which metals are won by electrolysis of molten chlorides. LO-6 alone, because the outcome already bands metals as low, medium and high reactivity, so the route-from-reactivity reasoning is internal to it; LO-2 is reserved for items that rank two named metals against each other.
Naming the metals that react violently with cold water is a top-of-series selection; the item is answered by ranking metals, so LO-2 rather than the single-metal LO-1 reading.
